\begin{frontmatter}

\title{Do knowledge-tracing simulators reward learning? A negative-control audit of reinforcement-learning exercise recommendation for programming}

\begin{abstract}
Reinforcement-learning (RL) agents that choose programming exercises are commonly trained and evaluated inside a knowledge-tracing (KT) model fitted to learner logs, which also measures their benefit. We audited this practice on {{n_interactions}} first attempts by {{n_learners}} learners of a C-programming online judge, none of whom were used before the study protocols were locked. Six learner models, including deep knowledge tracing (DKT), forecast held-out learners equally well (AUC {{auc_dkt2}}--{{auc_pfa}}), and an entropy-based identification tree gave interpretable diagnoses. DQN and PPO agents trained with a DKT reward exceeded random selection by {{abs_dqn_kt_insim}} and {{abs_ppo_kt_insim}} percentage points of expected post-test success in their training simulator, but by at most {{abs_max_latent_adv}} points in independently fitted worlds with explicit latent learning. In a negative-control world where learning is impossible, the DKT tracker still reported gains of {{abs_phantom_dqn_kt}} and {{abs_phantom_ppo_kt}} points for these agents, and across {{h3_n}} policies in-simulator gain was almost perfectly rank-correlated with this phantom gain (Spearman {{h3_rho}}). We show that a policy's expected gain inside a KT simulator equals the model's accumulated self-predicted change (drift), which is zero for coherent models without learning; DKT's drift was {{ratio_sd}} times more dispersed across problems than that of an additive factor model and was poorly reproduced by a re-seeded DKT. Agents trained in a world with explicit practice-driven learning transferred best across latent worlds of that family, but not to neural worlds. We recommend negative-control worlds, drift reporting and independently fitted worlds as standard checks for simulator-based evaluation of adaptive recommenders.
\end{abstract}

\begin{keyword}
knowledge tracing \sep reinforcement learning \sep exercise recommendation \sep programming education \sep simulation-based evaluation \sep negative control
\end{keyword}

\end{frontmatter}

\section{Proofs}\label{app:proofs}

\paragraph{Proof of \cref{prop:nodrift}} Write $\bar p(\theta)=|\mathcal W|^{-1}\sum_{k\in\mathcal W}p(y=1\mid k,\theta)$ and $\pi_H$ for the posterior of $\theta$ after history $H$. The model's forecasts are posterior predictive, $\bar P_M(H)=\int\bar p(\theta)\,\pi_H(\mathrm d\theta)$ and $P_M(y\mid j,H)=\int p(y\mid j,\theta)\,\pi_H(\mathrm d\theta)$. Because $\theta$ does not change with practice and outcomes are conditionally independent given $\theta$, Bayes' rule gives $\pi_{H\oplus(j,y)}(\mathrm d\theta)=p(y\mid j,\theta)\,\pi_H(\mathrm d\theta)/P_M(y\mid j,H)$. Hence
\begin{align}
\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}P_M(y\mid j,H)\,\bar P_M\bigl(H\oplus(j,y)\bigr)
&=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}\int\bar p(\theta)\,p(y\mid j,\theta)\,\pi_H(\mathrm d\theta)\notag\\
&=\int\bar p(\theta)\,\pi_H(\mathrm d\theta)=\bar P_M(H),
\end{align}
so $D_M(j,H)=0$. The argument holds for any prior, including the finite grid used for IRT in this study, whose per-problem drift was exactly zero (\cref{sec:res-h4}). $\square$

\paragraph{Proof of \cref{prop:insim}} Let $S_t=\bar P_M(H_{t+1})-\bar P_M(H_t)-D_M(j_t,H_t)$ be the surprise at step $t$. If $y_t$ is drawn from $P_M(\cdot\mid j_t,H_t)$, then by \cref{eq:drift}
\begin{align}
\mathbb E\bigl[S_t\mid H_t,j_t\bigr]
&=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}P_M(y\mid j_t,H_t)\,\bar P_M\bigl(H_t\oplus(j_t,y)\bigr)\notag\\
&\quad-\bar P_M(H_t)-D_M(j_t,H_t)=0.
\end{align}
The choice $j_t$ depends only on $H_t$ and on randomisation independent of future outcomes, so the tower property gives $\mathbb E[S_t]=0$ for every $t$. Taking expectations of \cref{eq:decomposition} yields the result. Combining both propositions, a coherent simulator without learning assigns an expected in-simulator gain of zero to every policy, and a simulator with learning ranks policies by the drift they accumulate. $\square$

\section{Implementation details}\label{app:impl}

\paragraph{Learner models} Logistic models: priors $\theta\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_\theta^2)$ with $\sigma_\theta\in\{0.4,0.5,0.6,0.75\}$ selected by inner-validation NLL, problem terms $\mathcal N(0,1)$, learning coefficients $\mathcal N(0,1)$; full-batch L-BFGS. DKT: embedding 32, LSTM 64, dropout 0.3 (0.1 on inputs), AdamW with weight decay $10^{-4}$, learning rate $10^{-3}$, batch 32, early stopping with patience 3 (maximum 30 epochs). SAKT: dimension 64, 4 heads, window 200, dropout 0.1. Problems attempted by at least 10 fitting learners receive their own parameters. ID3: minimum leaf size 200, minimum gain $10^{-3}$, maximum depth 6.

\paragraph{Agents} State: {{pool}} predicted success values, {{pool}} eligibility flags, 10 skill averages, post-test forecast and remaining horizon. Double DQN: two hidden layers of 256, replay 50,000, batch 256, learning rate $5\times10^{-4}$, soft target update $\tau=0.01$, $\varepsilon$ from 1 to 0.05 over half of training, $\gamma=0.99$. PPO: two hidden layers of 256 (tanh), learning rate $3\times10^{-4}$, 4 epochs, minibatch 128, clip 0.2, entropy 0.01, GAE $\lambda=0.95$. Each agent: 300 iterations of 64 parallel ten-step episodes; the final checkpoint is used; seeds 11, 23 and 37. Effort: after a failed first attempt, additional submissions follow a geometric distribution with the problem's mean from the world's partition (shrunk to the overall mean, capped at 10).

\section{Reproducibility}\label{app:repro}

Both protocols were locked before the evaluation population was loaded; the lock record lists SHA-256 hashes of protocols and code. Experiments ran through an append-only harness that snapshots protocol and source, records input and output hashes and refuses to overwrite a run. Run records: learner stage \texttt{{{learner_run_sha}}}\ldots, policy stage \texttt{{{policy_run_sha}}}\ldots\ (SHA-256 prefixes). Development and hyperparameter choices used a previously inspected cohort disjoint from the evaluation population. All numbers in this manuscript are inserted programmatically from the run outputs.

\section*{Data availability}
The ACcoding dataset is publicly available from its authors \citep{sun2026accodingdata,chen2024accoding}. Code, locked protocols, run records, aggregate results and the tables behind every figure will be deposited in a public repository upon acceptance (an anonymised copy is available to reviewers on request); learner-level derived files are not redistributed.

\section*{Ethics statement}
This is a secondary analysis of a public, anonymised dataset. No new data were collected and no learner was contacted or assigned to a condition.
